reference: FDA DI Q&A Q11 (e-signature satisfies the 'full signature, handwritten' wording); related Q3 (creating an electronic MPCR is a workflow to validate) and Q6 (MPCRs are controlled forms); binding basis 211.186(a); 21 CFR 11.2(a) with 11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200, 11.300
requirement: Binding (211.186(a), wording checked against the local CFR text): for each drug product and each batch size, one person prepares, dates and signs the MPCR and a second person independently checks, dates and signs it; MPCR preparation follows a written procedure. DI Q&A Q11: an electronic signature whose controls securely tie it to its record meets the handwritten full-signature wording (via 11.2(a)); Part 11 sets when e-signatures are legally equivalent, and firms should document the controls that let them identify the individual signer.
system_implications: Keep: author and independent checker e-signatures (different people), QA approval (its basis is 211.100(a)/211.22(c), not the DI Q&A), Effective-only issuance, in-flight batches stay on their issued version, change control for revisions. Add from the DI Q&A: each MBR version's steps, requirements and calculations are verified before it becomes Effective, because platform qualification does not show that a given MPCR is correct (Q3); MBR templates are issued only from the approved version under document control (Q6); the signer-identification controls are described in the validation file (Q11). Redline comparison and batch-size range handling are design or 211.186 matters outside the DI Q&A.
note: DI Q&A portion faithful to Q11 (line gave no Q number). The 211.186(a) wording matches the local CFR text. Added Q11's expectation to document signer-identification controls and the Q3/Q6 links relevant to the MBR lifecycle.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q6 (blank-form control, reconciliation, keeping spoiled forms); binding basis 211.188(a); document controls per 211.100, 211.160(a), 211.186; retention of replaced forms per 211.192, 211.194 (as cited in Q6)
requirement: Binding (211.188(a), checked against the local CFR text): every batch has a production and control record with complete information on its production and control, starting with an accurate reproduction of the applicable master record that has been checked for accuracy, dated and signed. DI Q&A Q6: document controls must exist; blank forms, if used (Q6 names electronic worksheets, lab notebooks and MPCRs), should fall under quality-unit control or some other document-control method; where appropriate, numbered sets may be issued and should be reconciled once all issued forms are completed; incomplete or erroneous forms should remain in the permanent record with a written reason for their replacement.
system_implications: Keep: issue only from the Effective MBR with version ID/hash stored; issuance signature; instructions frozen after issue with controlled amendments; unique numbering; issued/executed/voided reconciliation; voided or reissued instances retained with reason and approver. Clarify: Q6 presents numbered issuance as one option; the expectation is QU (or equivalent) document control, reconciliation and retention of replaced instances with written justification. Generating the batch record from the MBR is itself a workflow to validate (Q3).
note: Faithful to Q6 (line gave no Q number). Precision added: numbered issuance is an example, and control may be by the QU or another document-control method.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q1a-Q1f (definitions) and footnote 5; binding basis: ALCOA letters mapped to 211.101(d), 211.122, 211.186, 211.188(b)(11) (attributable), 211.180(e) (legible), 211.100(b), 211.160(a) (contemporaneous), 211.180, 211.194(a) (original/true copy), 211.22(a), 211.68, 211.188 (accurate); metadata retention 211.188, 211.194; backup 211.68(b), 211.180; systems 211.68
requirement: Q1a: data integrity means data are complete, consistent and accurate, and such data should show the ALCOA traits (Attributable; Legible; Contemporaneously recorded; Original or true copy; Accurate); the letters are listed, not individually defined. Integrity matters from first capture through use, storage and transfer to disposal after retention, and system design and controls should make errors, omissions and aberrant results easy to spot. Q1b: metadata is the context needed to make sense of a value (e.g., units, timestamps, who acquired it, which instrument, material identity/status, and audit trails); data should be retained for the full retention period with the metadata needed to reconstruct the activity, and the data-metadata link kept secure and traceable. Q1c: an audit trail is a secured, time-stamped electronic record generated by the computer itself, from which the creation, change or deletion of an electronic record can be reconstructed; it covers data-level changes and record/system-level actions such as access attempts or renaming/deleting files, and reprocessing should be documented with its justification. Q1d: static = fixed (paper, image); dynamic = the user can interact with the content (e.g., re-integrate a chromatogram, alter spreadsheet formulas that compute results or a calculated yield). Q1e: the 211.68(b) backup is a true copy of the original kept securely for the retention period, holding data plus metadata in the original or a compatible format; FDA equates it with an archive; temporary copies kept against crashes or interruptions do not meet 211.68(b). Q1f: 'computer or related systems' reach beyond software and servers to attached devices, networks, cloud hosting, the people who run them and their documentation (manuals, SOPs).
system_implications: Keep: each value stored with its metadata; dynamic data (historian trends, cycle data, spectra) kept natively with a viewer; the ALCOA-to-control mapping. Add: (1) audit trail entries are part of each value's metadata and must go with it into backup, archive, export and migration; (2) dispensing/charging metadata includes material identity and status; (3) in-system yield and other calculations are dynamic content - version-lock formulas and keep inputs, formula version and result (DI-NEW-03); (4) the 211.68(b) backup is a true copy with metadata and audit trails, in original or compatible format, kept for the full retention period; short-lived crash-recovery snapshots do not qualify, and a replica that mirrors deletions or corruption is not secure from alteration or loss; (5) hosting/cloud, network, peripherals, users and SOPs are within the 211.68 system (DI-NEW-04); (6) build detection of errors, omissions and aberrant results into the design (DI-NEW-01).
note: Stated points are accurate, but the line under-covered its own clause: Q1f (systems include cloud infrastructure, personnel, SOPs) was named but not paraphrased; audit trails being listed as metadata, the life-cycle and error-detection design expectation, and the backup = archive equivalence were missing. 'Must be kept with it' softened to 'should', with the binding hooks in 211.188/211.194.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q3; binding basis 211.63, 211.68(b), 211.110(a); MPCR-review analogy 211.100, 211.186
requirement: Yes: each CGMP workflow run on a computer system (FDA's example is building an electronic MPCR) is an intended use that should be checked through validation, with validation effort proportionate to the risk of the automated system. Qualifying a platform such as an MES shows it meets its own requirements but not that a particular MPCR it generates calculates correctly; validating the workflow shows the MPCR's steps, requirements and calculations work as intended - comparable to reviewing a paper MPCR and its supporting procedures before production use. If one system serves both CGMP and non-CGMP purposes, the firm should assess, and mitigate as appropriate, the chance that the non-CGMP features influence CGMP operations. Controls should cover software, hardware, personnel and documentation.
system_implications: Keep: validation of configured workflows, site configurations, interfaces and GMP-decision reports; every MBR version verified (steps, requirements, calculations) before it becomes Effective. Correct: a built-in MBR simulation/dry-run mode is a design choice, not an FDA expectation; if offered, it is a non-CGMP function inside a CGMP system and needs a documented assessment showing it cannot alter, leak into or be mistaken for real batch records (segregated data, visible marking, no real lot IDs, never used with actual product samples - cf. Q13). Scale validation depth to risk; validate review-by-exception rules because Q8 expects review reliability to be demonstrable; include hardware, personnel (roles, training) and documentation in scope.
note: Faithful to Q3 (now checked against the primary text, so the 'secondary summaries' caveat can be dropped). Added the risk-proportionate extent, the CGMP/non-CGMP coexistence point and the four control elements; system implications trimmed where a product feature was presented as required.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q4; binding basis 211.68(b) (changes only by authorized personnel)
requirement: Must (211.68(b)): controls ensuring only authorized personnel can change computerized MPCRs or other CGMP records or enter laboratory data into computerized records; Q4 extends the restricted-control expectation to records from automated visual inspection, electronic materials management and automated dispensing/weighing systems. Should: technically limit, where feasible, who can change specifications, process parameters, data, or manufacturing and testing methods (e.g., through permissions over settings and data); give the system administrator role, including rights over files and settings, to people independent of those responsible for record content; establish a documented record of each CGMP system's authorized users and their privileges (e.g., a maintained list).
system_implications: Keep: IT/configuration administration segregated from GMP data roles; specifications, process parameters and MBR content editable only via the MBR/master-data change workflow; privileged activity logged and periodically reviewed. Add: weighing/dispensing, materials-management and visual-inspection data are explicitly in scope; restriction covers data generally, not only process-parameter data; current and historical user/role/privilege listing per system (DI-NEW-06). Correct: FDA gives no small-site fallback - a one-person admin-plus-QA exception with secondary review is a firm-defined compensating control needing its own justification, not an FDA recommendation.
note: Q number supplied (Q4). Removed 'where that is not possible, secondary review is recommended': no such fallback exists in the final Dec 2018 text, and the line's 'FDA suggests' wording differs from the final 'should' (likely draft-era or other-guidance wording); similar compensating-control language exists in other DI guidance (e.g., PIC/S PI 041, MHRA GXP DI) - confirm there before citing. Fixed 'process parameter data' (Q4 lists process parameters and data separately). Added Q4's record examples and the documented access-privilege list.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q5; binding basis 211.100, 211.68(b), 211.188(b)(11), 211.194(a)(7)-(8) (actions attributable to a specific individual)
requirement: With shared login credentials the login cannot identify a unique individual, so the system would not meet the part 211/212 CGMP requirements; system and documentation controls must be designed to assure product quality (211.100), and actions such as changing records or entering data must be traceable to one specific person (211.68(b), 211.188(b)(11), 211.194(a)(7)-(8)). Read-only accounts shared among users, which cannot alter data or settings, may be used just to look at data, but not for actions such as second-person review, which must be attributable to one individual.
system_implications: Keep: no shared or generic accounts for any GMP action, including line logins; fast individual re-authentication on shared terminals; individual authentication per GMP entry in kiosk mode; interface/service accounts non-interactive, unable to sign, attributed to the device or interface. Add: a shared read-only view (e.g., line status display) is acceptable only if it technically cannot create, change, sign, verify or acknowledge anything; every review or verification action requires individual authentication.
note: Q number supplied (Q5). The sentence that audit trails cannot be relied on with shared logins is a reasonable inference but is not stated in Q5, so it is no longer presented as FDA text. Added the read-only shared-account allowance and the binding clauses FDA cites.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q6; binding basis 211.100, 211.160(a), 211.186 (document controls required); 211.192, 211.194 (retaining replaced forms)
requirement: Must: document controls that assure product quality are in place. Should: blank forms, if used - Q6 explicitly names electronic worksheets, laboratory notebooks and MPCRs - be controlled by the quality unit or another document-control method (bound, paginated, officially stamped notebooks are cited as good practice because unofficial books and missing pages stand out); where appropriate, issue numbered sets and reconcile them once all issued forms are completed; retain spoiled or incomplete forms in the permanent record together with a written reason they were replaced; keep all data needed to recreate the CGMP activity in the complete record.
system_implications: Keep: controlled issuance of batch record instances, logbooks and ad-hoc forms from approved template versions; unique numbering; issued/completed/voided reconciliation; voided instances retained and retrievable with reason. Adjust: QA approval of every void is a firm choice - Q6 asks for a written justification under QU or other document control, not QA sign-off per void. Spreadsheets or electronic worksheets used to produce CGMP data are controlled forms (Q6 names electronic worksheets); uncontrolled attachments may be kept only as clearly labelled supporting information and never as the source of a CGMP result.
note: Faithful to Q6 (Q number supplied). Added that 'electronic worksheets' are named explicitly - important for an eBMR - and the complete-record sentence.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q7 (who) and Q8 (how often), footnote 13; binding basis 211.192 (QU reviews and approves all production and control records, audit trails included, before release), 211.22, 211.188(b) (each significant step); also 211.101(c)-(d), 211.103, 211.182, 211.186(a), 211.194(a)(8) as cited in Q7
requirement: Q7: audit trail review is comparable to examining cross-outs on paper; whoever is responsible for reviewing a CGMP record should review the audit trails of changes to that record's data during the same review; the quality unit must review and approve every production and control record, audit trails being part of those records (211.192); some review may be done by the person directly supervising or checking a step (211.188); FDA advises overseeing and reviewing CGMP records through a quality-system approach. Q8: where CGMP regulations fix a review frequency for the data, use the same frequency for its audit trail - for batch records, review after each significant step (211.188(b)) and before batch release (211.22); otherwise set the frequency from process knowledge and a risk assessment of data criticality, control mechanisms and product-quality impact; the approach must satisfy CGMP and its reliability should be proven. Footnote 13 names risks such as unauthorized or undetected deletion, amendment or exclusion, and offers logs of instrument status and communications, and alerts, as candidates for risk-based review.
system_implications: Keep: mandatory QA release-review section listing post-entry changes (old/new value, who, when, reason) with release blocked until reviewed; step verifiers see changes to the data they verify; drill-down to the full audit trail; periodic recorded system-level review. Correct: (1) step and release reviews cover changes to all data in the batch record, not only fields the MBR designer flags as critical - criticality may prioritise or highlight, not exclude; (2) the frequency for system and interface logs (logins, permissions, configuration, equipment communication, alarms) comes from a documented risk assessment of criticality, controls and product impact, not 'system complexity'; (3) validate the review-by-exception filters so review reliability can be shown (DI-NEW-08); (4) show changes inline like paper cross-outs, old value visible beside the new.
note: Split into Q7 and Q8. The phrases 'critical data reviewed with each record and before final approval' and 'schedule based on system complexity and intended use' are not in the final Dec 2018 text (likely carried over from the 2016 draft); the final ties audit trail review frequency to the regulatory review frequency of the underlying data (each significant step and before release, for batch records) or to a documented risk assessment.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q12 and footnote 14; binding basis 211.100(b), 211.160(a) (documented at the time of performance), 211.180(d)
requirement: Any data created to meet a CGMP requirement is a CGMP record and must be documented or saved when the activity is performed (211.100(b), 211.160(a)). FDA expects processes designed so that required data cannot be changed unless the change itself is recorded (its lab example: write to durable media as each step or injection finishes, including incomplete or aborted ones, rather than at the end of a set; audit-trail changes and investigate aborted runs). Jotting data on scrap paper for later transcription is not acceptable, and neither is any electronic storage that lets records be manipulated before a permanent record exists. Technical and procedural controls may be combined - e.g., an EBR or LIMS that commits automatically after every entry (the electronic counterpart of indelible, contemporaneous entries on a paper batch record) plus a procedure requiring data to be entered as soon as generated. Footnote 14: FDA also reviews records not intended for CGMP that contain CGMP information.
system_implications: Keep: durable server-side commit with audit trail at each entry; no silent draft state for GMP observations; post-commit edits are audit-trailed changes with reason; offline clients use a tamper-evident append-only journal that syncs with original timestamps (engineering choice). Add: an SOP requiring immediate entry at the point of work (Q12 pairs technical and procedural controls); no free-text scratch fields later transcribed into GMP fields; outages handled with controlled, pre-issued contingency forms (DI-NEW-12), never ad-hoc notes; aborted or interrupted operations captured and justified (DI-NEW-13). Automatic instrument capture is good practice, not an explicit Q12 requirement.
note: The 'temporary memory' sentences are not in the final Dec 2018 text (likely draft-era wording). The final states a broader rule - no storage method may allow manipulation before a permanent record exists - and adds that required data must not be changeable without a record of the change, plus the scrap-paper prohibition. Q number supplied.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q9 (true copies) and Q10 (printouts vs dynamic originals); binding basis 211.180(d) (original records or true copies; suitable reader available), 211.68(b), 211.188, 211.194, 211.194(a)(8)
requirement: Q9: yes, electronic copies may serve as true copies of records originally on paper or in electronic form if they keep the original's content and meaning - all metadata needed to reconstruct the activity and the original's static or dynamic nature; true copies of dynamic records may be kept in the original format or another format that preserves content and meaning, provided suitable reader and copying equipment (software, hardware, media readers) remains readily available. Q10: a printout or static record can meet retention requirements when it is itself the original or a true copy - e.g., balances and pH meters that print at acquisition, in which case the printout or a true copy must be kept (211.180); for instruments whose records are dynamic (e.g., a reprocessable FT-IR spectral file), a printout or static record does not satisfy 211.180(d), and a partial spectrum display could hide contaminants. Original lab records, paper or electronic, must receive second-person review (211.194(a)(8)).
system_implications: Keep: native archival and export of dynamic data (historian series, cycle data, images, spectra) with metadata; interactive re-rendering test. Add: keep a validated viewer for the full retention period or migrate to a format that keeps content and meaning (DI-NEW-09); where a balance or similar device prints a ticket that is the original, retain it (or a true copy) linked to the eBMR entry, or capture the value electronically so the electronic record is the original (DI-NEW-10). Correct: a verifier signature for scanned true copies and conditions for destroying paper originals are reasonable firm controls but are not described in the DI Q&A.
note: Faithful (Q9 + Q10; Q numbers supplied). Added that a static printout can be the original for simple devices such as balances and pH meters - directly relevant to eBMR weighing - and the reader-availability condition.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q11; binding basis 211.186(a); 21 CFR 11.2(a), with Part 11 signature controls 11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200, 11.300
requirement: Yes: electronic signatures with appropriate controls may stand in for handwritten signatures or initials in any record CGMP requires; for the handwritten full-signature wording of 211.186(a), an electronic signature with controls that securely link it to its record meets the requirement (11.2(a)); Part 11 sets the criteria for legal equivalence. Firms should document the controls that let them identify the specific person who signed. PET MPCRs (part 212) have no handwritten-signature requirement.
system_implications: Keep: paperless MPCR preparation/check/approval, execution and release once Part 11 signature controls are met; initials fields use the same mechanism. Add: the validation file documents the signer-identification controls (unique IDs, identity verification before credential issue, signature manifestation, signature-record linking).
note: Faithful to Q11 (Q number supplied). Added the expectation to document signer-identification controls.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q2 (with Q13 on retaining all data and testing into compliance); binding basis 211.22, 211.180 (QU evaluation, retention), 211.160(b), 211.188, 211.192 (scientifically sound justification and investigation)
requirement: The quality unit must assess all data generated within a CGMP record when deciding on release, and those data are retained for CGMP purposes; electronic data include the metadata needed to reconstruct the activity. Excluding test results from QU decisions on conformance to a specification needs a valid, documented, scientifically sound justification (see the OOS guidance). Even after legitimate invalidation based on a scientifically sound investigation, the complete batch record handed to the QU still carries the invalidated original data plus the investigation report. Retention and review requirements are the same for paper and electronic records. Q13 adds that every result - obvious errors, failing, passing and suspect - must be retained and reviewed, and invalidation needs an investigation.
system_implications: Keep: invalidation never deletes; the value is marked invalid with justification, user and timestamp and stays visible in the record and exception list. Correct: invalidating a genuine measurement must link to a documented investigation (deviation/OOS-type record) whose report is part of the QU release package - the QU sees invalidated data and the report at release (Q2), not only 'QA concurrence where the SOP says so'; distinguish correcting an entry error (audit-trailed change with reason, still retained per Q13) from invalidating a real result (investigation). Repeat-until-pass flagging is supported by Q13 (DI-NEW-14); a fixed 'three repeats' threshold is a design choice.
note: Q number supplied (Q2). Added the investigation-report element and QU evaluation of all CGMP data at release; 'cannot be deleted or selectively reported' is a fair synthesis of Q2 and Q13 rather than Q2 wording. Q2 speaks of test results versus specifications; applying it to IPC/production data is a reasonable extension.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q17 (and footnote 14 to Q12); binding basis 211.180(c) (records available for authorized inspection and copying), FD&C Act 704
requirement: Every record required under CGMP is open to FDA inspection, including records created and kept on computerized systems and electronic communications that support CGMP activities (FDA's example: an email authorizing batch release is a CGMP record). Firms must permit authorized inspection and review, and copying of records including electronic data (211.180(c)). Footnote 14: FDA routinely asks for records not intended to meet a CGMP requirement that still contain CGMP information (e.g., shipping records used to reconstruct an activity). Metadata and audit trails are covered because Q1b and Q7 treat them as part of the record.
system_implications: Keep: ability to provide read-only, audited, time-limited viewing access and to generate complete export packages (data, metadata, audit trails) quickly. Add: exports usable as electronic copies (native/structured, not only PDF) so electronic data can be copied; keep release and other GMP approvals inside the eBMR with e-signatures so informal channels are not the approval record, and retain any that are used (DI-NEW-18). Correct: a dedicated inspector account is a design option, not an FDA expectation (firm staff often operate the system; Q5 allows shared read-only viewing, though individual accounts are preferable); SLA targets and remote-assessment support come from other sources.
note: Q number supplied (Q17). The DI Q&A does not mention 704(a)(4) record requests, remote regulatory assessments or the 2025 RRA guidance; these cannot be verified from the local files and must be cited to their own sources. Added the duty to allow copying of electronic data and the electronic-communications point.

reference: Composite. DI Q&A support: Q1a (ALCOA), Q1b (audit trails are metadata kept for the retention period), Q1c (audit trail definition; data not lost or obscured), Q1e (backup), Q5 (attributable), Q11 (signature securely linked), Q12 (saved at time of performance; no change without a record); binding basis 11.10(e), 11.70, 211.68(b), 211.100(b), 211.180
requirement: The composite is consistent with the DI Q&A and the cited rules: records attributable and contemporaneous (211.100(b); Q1a, Q5, Q12); changes must not obscure earlier entries (11.10(e); Q1c, Q12); audit trails secure, computer-generated, time-stamped and retained at least as long as the records (11.10(e); Q1b); signatures linked so they cannot be removed, copied or moved to falsify a record (11.70; Q11); backups exact, complete and protected from alteration, erasure or loss (211.68(b); Q1e).
system_implications: The append-only/event-sourced store, hash chaining, trusted time source, UTC storage with local rendering, DST tests and DBA-tamper detection are engineering choices not found in the DI Q&A (it says nothing about clocks, time zones or hashing); keep them labelled as design decisions. DBA segregation is supported by Q4 (administrators independent of record content). Correct one risk: blocking data capture on clock drift must come with a controlled contingency (issued contingency forms, Q6; DI-NEW-12) so operators never fall back on scrap-paper notes, which Q12 rejects; log the drift event and the affected entries for review.
note: Requirement faithful to the Q&A and cited rules. System implications marked as beyond the guidance, and one conflict corrected: blocking capture without a controlled fallback would work against Q12's contemporaneous-recording expectation.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q1a (ALCOA letter, not defined) and footnote 5; usage in Background, Q1b, Q5; binding basis 211.101(d), 211.122, 211.186, 211.188(b)(11), 212.50(c)(10); for actions and review also 211.68(b), 211.194(a)(7)-(8)
requirement: FDA use: one of the five ALCOA traits that complete, consistent and accurate data should show; the guidance gives no stand-alone definition and instead points to the regulations listed. Meaning shown by use: the Background asks whether activities can be traced to a specific individual; Q5 says shared logins prevent identifying a unique person and that record changes and reviews must be attributable to one individual; Q1b lists user ID and instrument ID as metadata.
system_implications: Individual accounts for every GMP action; user ID (and device/instrument ID and timestamp where relevant) stored with each value and change; data from automated equipment attributed to the device and to the person who checks the automated step (211.188(b)(11)).
note: The line's FDA claim is correct. The 'meaning' text is an EU-style definition; the cited EU GMP Chapter 4 July 2025 draft is not among the local files (only the 2011 Chapter 4, which has no ALCOA definitions), so it could not be verified here. FDA's focus is the individual; 'what system/instrument' is consistent with Q1b metadata.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q1a (ALCOA letter, not defined) and footnote 5; related Q1c, Q9; binding basis 211.180(e), 212.110(b)
requirement: FDA use: listed in ALCOA with no definition; footnote 5 points to 211.180(e) and 212.110(b). Related text: Q1c says good record-keeping keeps data from being lost or obscured; Q9 requires copies to keep content and meaning and a suitable reader to remain available.
system_implications: Human-readable rendering of values, units and codes; corrections never overwrite (the prior value stays visible); viewers remain usable for the retention period.
note: FDA claim correct. 'Corrections must not hide the original' rests on Q1c and 11.10(e), not on an FDA definition of legible. EU source not verifiable locally.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q1a ('contemporaneously recorded') and footnote 5; applied in Q12; binding basis 211.100(b), 211.160(a)
requirement: FDA use: the ALCOA trait is worded 'contemporaneously recorded', which footnote 5 explains as recorded at the time of performance (211.100(b), 211.160(a)). Q12 applies it: data must be documented or saved when the work is done; an EBR that commits after every entry plus a procedure for immediate entry is an acceptable approach; transcribing from scrap paper is not.
system_implications: Server-side commit and timestamp at each entry; SOP for immediate entry; no deferred bulk entry. Trusted-clock synchronisation and late-entry flags are sensible design controls but are not mentioned in the FDA guidance.
note: FDA claim correct. Trusted clock and late-entry flagging are design additions, not FDA text. EU source not verifiable locally.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q1a ('original or a true copy') and footnote 5; Q9, Q10, Q12; binding basis 211.180 (esp. 211.180(d)), 211.194(a)
requirement: FDA use: ALCOA's 'O' is 'original or a true copy' (211.180, 211.194(a)); there is no separate definition of original. A true copy must keep content and meaning, including the metadata needed to reconstruct the activity and whether the original was static or dynamic (Q9). A printout can itself be the original for simple devices such as balances and pH meters, but for dynamic records a printout or static image does not qualify as original or true copy (Q10). FDA uses 'true copy', not 'certified copy', and prescribes no particular copy-verification procedure.
system_implications: Name the original record for each data type; retain first-capture electronic data natively; any copying process (scan, export, migration) preserves metadata and dynamic nature; PDF renderings of dynamic data are views, not replacements.
note: FDA claim correct. 'Verified true/certified copy' is EU/PIC/S terminology; FDA's term is true copy. Added the Q10 nuance that static printouts can be originals. EU source not verifiable locally.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q1a (in the DI definition and as ALCOA's final letter) and footnote 5; Q3; binding basis 211.22(a), 211.68 (incl. 211.68(b) input/output checks), 211.188, 212.60(g)
requirement: FDA use: accuracy appears both in the definition of data integrity and as the last ALCOA letter, with no stand-alone definition. Footnote 5 ties it to QU review authority (211.22(a)), computer input/output checks and backup (211.68) and complete batch records (211.188). Q3 illustrates it: validating the workflow shows that the MPCR's calculations are right.
system_implications: Validated calculations and interfaces; input/output verification scaled to system complexity and reliability (211.68(b)); one-person verification of automated steps where 211.101, 211.103 or 211.188(b)(11) apply (211.68(c)); corrections only through audit-trailed changes.
note: FDA claim correct. Calibrated instruments and verification of critical manual entries in the 'meaning' are consistent with CGMP but are not described in the DI Q&A. EU source not verifiable locally.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q1a (completeness is part of the DI definition, not an ALCOA letter); Background, Q2, Q6, Q13, Q14; binding basis 211.188, 211.194, 212.60(g)
requirement: FDA use: completeness is one of three properties in the definition of data integrity (with consistency and accuracy), not an ALCOA letter, and has no separate definition. The idea runs through the text: the Background cites the complete-record requirements of 211.188 and 211.194; Q2 puts invalidated data and the investigation report into the batch record the QU reviews; Q6 keeps spoiled forms and all data needed to recreate the activity; Q13 requires all results, including errors and failures, to be retained and reviewed; Q14 keeps every reprocessing result.
system_implications: Nothing deleted or hidden; repeats, failures, invalidated and aborted entries kept and shown to reviewers; completeness checks before step and batch sign-off; metadata and audit trails retained as part of the record.
note: FDA claim correct. The 'meaning' is consistent with Q2/Q6/Q13. EU and EMA GCP sources not verifiable locally.

reference: FDA DI Q&A Q1a (consistency is part of the DI definition, not an ALCOA letter); no binding clause mapped (footnote 5 covers only the ALCOA letters)
requirement: FDA use: consistency appears only in the definition of data integrity; the guidance gives no definition, examples or regulatory mapping for it.
system_implications: Uniform units and formats and correctly ordered timestamps are reasonable design controls (they also serve Q1a's call for designs that make errors, omissions and aberrant results easy to spot), but the specific meaning in the line is not FDA's.
note: FDA claim correct; the 'uniform, logical sequence' meaning comes from other sources, not the FDA Q&A. EU source not verifiable locally.

reference: Not an FDA DI Q&A term. Related: Q1b (retain data with metadata for the retention period), Q1e (backup kept securely for the retention period), Q9 (reader availability), Background (data kept secure from creation to disposition); binding basis 211.68(b), 211.180, 212.110(b)
requirement: The FDA guidance neither uses nor defines 'enduring'. Durability is expressed as: keep data and metadata for the whole retention period (Q1b); keep a secure true-copy backup in original or compatible format for that period (Q1e); protect data from creation through disposition (Background); for PET, store records to prevent deterioration or loss (212.110(b), quoted in the Background).
system_implications: Durable, protected storage and verified backups/archives for the full retention period; lossless, verified format migration.
note: The line did not claim FDA usage; confirmed that FDA does not define this ALCOA+ term. EU/EMA sources not verifiable locally.

reference: Not an FDA DI Q&A term. Related: Q9 (suitable reader and copying equipment readily available), Q17 (records open to FDA inspection and copying), Q2 (data evaluated by the QU at release); binding basis 211.180(c), 211.180(d)
requirement: The FDA guidance does not use or define 'available' as a data integrity principle. The idea appears as: a suitable reader must be readily available for true copies of dynamic records (Q9; 211.180(d)); CGMP records, electronic ones included, must be open to FDA inspection, review and copying (Q17; 211.180(c)); the QU evaluates the data at release (Q2).
system_implications: Records retrievable and readable throughout retention, including after upgrades or decommissioning; exports that support inspection copying.
note: The line did not claim FDA usage; confirmed that FDA does not define this ALCOA+ term. EU/EMA GCP sources not verifiable locally.

reference: Not an FDA ALCOA term; the word appears once, in Q1b (data-metadata relationships kept secure and traceable); related Q1c (audit trail enables reconstruction)
requirement: FDA does not list traceable as a data integrity principle. It uses the word only when saying the relationship between data and their metadata should be kept secure and traceable (Q1b); reconstruction of a record's history comes from the audit trail definition (Q1c).
system_implications: Persistent identifiers linking values, metadata, audit trail entries and signatures, surviving archive and migration, so any record's history can be reconstructed end to end.
note: The line is right that Traceable is not in the FDA 2018 ALCOA list; added that FDA does use 'traceable' for data-metadata relationships (Q1b). The EU Chapter 4 July 2025 draft (ALCOA++) is not in the local files, so that source could not be verified.

reference: Q1a (whole life cycle; design for detection); binding basis 211.68(b) (input/output checked for accuracy), 211.188, 211.192
requirement: Data integrity should hold from first capture through use, storage and transfer to disposal after the retention period, and system design and controls should make errors, omissions and aberrant results easy to spot throughout (recommendation; the binding hooks are the 211.68(b) accuracy checks and the record-review duties in 211.188/211.192).
system_implications: Real-time checks against MBR limits and expected ranges; mandatory-entry and step-completeness checks before sign-off; detection of out-of-sequence or late entries; reconciliation of interface transfers (eBMR to ERP/LIMS/historian) by counts or checksums; an exception list feeding step and QA review; integrity check on archive retrieval.
verification_test: Seed a test batch with an out-of-limit value, a skipped mandatory entry, an out-of-order timestamp and a dropped interface message: each is flagged and appears in the review exception list; restoring an archived batch passes the integrity check.

reference: Q1b (audit trails count as metadata; data-metadata link secure and traceable), Q1c (audit trail scope; justification for reprocessing); binding basis 11.10(e); 211.68(b), 211.188, 211.194
requirement: Audit trails should let reviewers reconstruct how each electronic record was created, changed or deleted, covering data-level events (e.g., parameters, results) and record/system-level events (e.g., access attempts, renaming or deleting files); FDA's HPLC example expects who ran it, when, the processing settings, and any reprocessing with its reason. Audit trails are themselves metadata, to be retained with the data for the retention period with the relationship kept secure. Binding: 11.10(e) requires secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails of operator entries and actions, kept as long as the records.
system_implications: Each GMP audit entry holds user, timestamp, record and field, old and new value, action type and reason for change; a protected system log records logins and failed logins, role and permission changes, configuration changes, voids and deletion attempts; audit trails are immutable, archived with the batch record, and readable by reviewers in plain language.
verification_test: Change a recorded value -> audit shows who, when, old, new and reason; a failed login, a role change and a configuration change each appear in the system log; an archived batch restores with its complete audit trail.

reference: Q1d (spreadsheet formulas computing results or a calculated yield are dynamic content), Q3 (validated MPCR calculations), Q6 (electronic worksheets are controlled forms); binding basis 211.103, 211.188(b)(7), 211.68(b)
requirement: FDA gives spreadsheet formulas that compute results or a calculated yield as an example of dynamic record content (Q1d); workflow validation should show MPCR calculations are correct (Q3); electronic worksheets are forms to control (Q6). Binding: yields are determined at appropriate phases and, when an automated system under 211.68 computes them, one person independently verifies the result (211.103); the batch record states actual and percent-of-theoretical yield (211.188(b)(7)); computer input and output are checked for accuracy (211.68(b)).
system_implications: Yield and other GMP calculations run in validated, version-controlled eBMR logic, storing inputs, formula version and result; one person verifies each automated yield calculation as 211.103 requires; any external spreadsheet used for GMP calculations is a controlled template, retained natively with formulas intact as a dynamic record, not only as a printout.
verification_test: The yield step shows inputs, formula version, result and a verification signature; editing a formula outside change control is impossible; an attached spreadsheet is a controlled template version stored in native format.

reference: Q1f; binding basis 211.68(a)-(b)
requirement: For 211.68, 'computer or related systems' means more than software and servers: FDA includes attached devices, networks, cloud hosting, the people who operate the system and its documentation such as manuals and SOPs (drawing on an ANSI description of a system as people, machines and methods organized for set functions).
system_implications: Validation, access control, change control and backup scope for the eBMR cover the hosting/cloud and network layers, peripherals (balances, scanners, label printers, terminals), interfaces, user roles and training, and the SOPs/manuals. For SaaS or cloud hosting, assess the provider's controls over these layers and cover them contractually (design inference - Q1f names cloud infrastructure but does not detail supplier controls).
verification_test: The system inventory/validation plan lists hosting and cloud components, network, peripherals, interfaces, roles and SOPs, each with an owner and qualification evidence; a change to a hosting component is routed through change control.

requirement: When one system handles both CGMP and non-CGMP work, the firm should assess, and mitigate as appropriate, the chance that its non-CGMP features influence CGMP operations; the extent of validation should match the risk the automated system poses, and controls should address software, hardware, personnel and documentation.
system_implications: Documented impact assessment for non-GMP features (training or sandbox tenants, MBR simulation, planning/scheduling, analytics, ERP sync); their data segregated; they cannot write to GMP records, change GMP configuration or produce output that could be mistaken for GMP records (visible non-GMP marking).
verification_test: Attempt to write from the training/simulation area into a production batch record, or to reuse a real lot number there -> blocked; non-GMP outputs carry a non-GMP watermark; the impact assessment is in the validation package.

reference: Q4; binding basis 211.68(b)
requirement: Manufacturers should set up and use a way of documenting which personnel are authorized on each CGMP computer system and with what privileges (e.g., a maintained list of authorized individuals), supporting the binding 211.68(b) duty that only authorized personnel make changes.
system_implications: The eBMR reports current and point-in-time users, roles, privileges and sites, with who granted or removed each privilege and when; access changes follow an approved request workflow; periodic access reviews record reviewer and outcome.
verification_test: Produce the access list as of a past date and reconcile it with access-request records; remove a leaver's access -> reflected in the list and the audit trail immediately.

reference: Inference from Q4 (technical restriction of settings changes; administrators independent of record content), Q12 (no change to required data without a record), Q1c; binding basis 11.10(e), 211.68(b)
requirement: The DI Q&A does not explicitly say who may switch audit trails off. It does recommend technically restricting who can change settings and reserving administrator rights over files and settings for people independent of record content (Q4), and it expects required data to be unchangeable without a record of the change (Q12); Part 11 requires secure, computer-generated audit trails of record creation, modification and deletion (11.10(e), binding). Together these mean audit trailing of GMP records should never be something that users responsible for record content can disable.
system_implications: GMP audit trail permanently on and not configurable per user, batch or step; any audit-scope setting changeable only by independent administrators through change control, with the change itself logged in a protected system log and flagged for QA review; no role that enters, verifies, reviews or releases GMP data holds that right.
verification_test: As a production or QA user, look for any function to disable or narrow audit trailing -> none exists; as administrator, change an audit-related setting -> requires a change-control reference and appears in the system log and the next periodic review.

reference: Q8 and footnote 13; binding basis 211.68(b), 211.192
requirement: Where the regulations fix no review frequency for a kind of data, derive the audit-trail review frequency from process knowledge and a risk assessment of data criticality, control mechanisms and product-quality impact, considering risks such as deletion, amendment or exclusion without authorization or detection; FDA's examples for risk-based review are logs of instrument status and communications, and alerts. The approach should meet CGMP and its reliability should be demonstrated.
system_implications: Capture and retain equipment/instrument interface logs (connection loss, message failures, retries), equipment status and alarm/alert records with the batch; a documented risk assessment sets their review frequency; events affecting a batch surface in that batch's review; the review-by-exception logic is validated and periodically challenged (e.g., comparing sampled full audit trails with the filtered view).
verification_test: Interrupt a balance or equipment interface during a step -> the event is recorded, linked to the batch and shown in review; the risk assessment defining frequency is on file; a periodic review record exists; a seeded unauthorized change is caught by the exception filter.

requirement: Copies of dynamic electronic records can count as true copies when held in the original format or in one that keeps content and meaning, as long as a suitable reader and copying equipment (software, hardware, media readers) stays readily available (211.180(d)); backups/archives are true copies with metadata kept for the whole retention period (Q1e).
system_implications: Archive plan covers the full retention period (at least one year after batch expiry under 211.180(a), longer if firm policy requires); keep a validated viewer or migrate to a format that preserves content, meaning, metadata and interactivity, verifying each migration; retiring a system requires a documented migration or read-only retention plan.
verification_test: Restore and interactively view the oldest retained batch (trends and audit trail included); a migration verification report shows record counts, checksums and sample comparisons.

reference: Q12 (data are a CGMP record when generated), Q10 (printouts as originals vs dynamic records), Q2 (same rules for paper and electronic); binding basis 211.180, 211.180(d), 211.188, 211.194
requirement: Data generated to meet a CGMP requirement are a CGMP record from the moment of generation (Q12). A printout or static record can be the original for devices such as balances and pH meters, and then it or a true copy must be kept (Q10, 211.180); dynamic electronic records cannot be replaced by printouts (Q10). Retention and review requirements do not differ between paper and electronic records (Q2).
system_implications: For each data type define the original: values keyed or captured in the eBMR are electronic originals and PDFs/prints are copies; device printouts that are originals are either retained and linked to the eBMR entry (reference number, reconciliation) or replaced by direct electronic capture; hybrid paper components get the same review and retention as the electronic record.
verification_test: The data-flow map for each MBR names the original record per data source; a weighing with a printed ticket shows the ticket linked and retained (or direct capture configured); a PDF export of the eBMR is marked as a copy.

reference: Q10 (second-person review of original lab records; microbiology plate-count example); binding basis 211.194(a)(8); for production steps 211.188(b)(11)
requirement: Original laboratory records, paper or electronic, must get second-person review so that all results and related information are properly reported (211.194(a)(8)); FDA's example is a contemporaneous written record of petri-dish colony counts that a second person then reviews.
system_implications: Manual readings entered in the eBMR (e.g., environmental monitoring plate counts, visual checks, manual gauge readings) are entered at the time of reading by the reader and verified by a different person; the record shows reader, verifier and both timestamps. For production steps the binding hook is 211.188(b)(11) (performer and checker identified).
verification_test: Enter a plate count -> second-person verification is required and the same user cannot verify their own entry; the record shows reader, verifier and timestamps.

reference: Q12 (no scrap-paper transcription), Q6 (controlled blank forms); binding basis 211.100(b), 211.160(a), 211.180(d), 211.186
requirement: Writing data on loose scraps that are thrown away once copied into the permanent record is not acceptable (Q12); blank forms that are used should be controlled and reconciled, with spoiled forms retained with justification (Q6).
system_implications: Provide a controlled contingency process for eBMR or network outages: pre-approved, uniquely numbered contingency forms issued under QU/document control; entries made on them at the time of performance; after recovery, the data are entered or attached as verified true copies, the paper originals retained, issued forms reconciled and the contingency period reviewed; no ad-hoc notes or personal devices.
verification_test: Simulate an outage: contingency forms are issued and logged; after recovery the batch shows the contingency period, linked scanned originals, reconciliation of issued forms and reviewer sign-off.

reference: Q12 (lab example: save each step or injection including aborted ones; aborted/incomplete injections audit-trailed, investigated, justified) - applied by analogy; binding basis 211.100(b), 211.188, 211.192
requirement: FDA expects processes designed so that required data cannot be changed without a record; in its chromatography example, data are written to durable media as each step or injection completes (incomplete or aborted ones included), and aborted or incomplete injections are captured in audit trails, investigated and justified.
system_implications: By analogy: aborted, cancelled or interrupted eBMR operations (abandoned weighings, cancelled label prints, aborted equipment cycles, restarted steps) are recorded with who, when and reason, remain visible in the batch record and need justification or investigation before step completion or release.
verification_test: Abort a weighing midway and restart -> both attempts recorded and the aborted one requires a reason; cancel a label print -> recorded and reconciled; the review view lists all aborted events.

reference: Q13 (applied by analogy to in-process testing); binding basis 211.160, 211.165, 211.188, 211.192, 211.194, 211.68(b)
requirement: Sampling or testing aimed at obtaining a particular result or overcoming an unacceptable one (so-called testing into compliance) conflicts with CGMP, and running actual samples in test, prep or equilibration runs to disguise it is violative. If an actual sample is used for system suitability, it should be a characterized secondary standard from a different batch, under written procedures. Every result, including plain mistakes and failing, suspect or passing values, has to stay in the retained CGMP records and be reviewed; invalidation needs an investigation with a documented, scientifically sound justification.
system_implications: No unrecorded 'trial', 'practice' or 'check' measurements on product samples: every IPC measurement on product (repeats, failures and aborted readings included) is captured in the batch record and shown to reviewers; equipment set-up and suitability checks use registered standards, recorded separately and never under a product sample ID; repeat-until-pass patterns and discarded readings are flagged; retests follow an SOP with an investigation link.
verification_test: Take three IPC readings on one sample where the first two fail -> all three recorded and flagged; try an instrument 'test' mode with a product sample ID -> blocked or recorded in the batch; a suitability check requires a registered standard ID.

reference: Q14 (applied by analogy to production calculations and in-line data); binding basis 211.160, 211.165(c), 211.194(a)(4), 211.194(a); for production 211.188
requirement: Saving only the final result of reprocessed lab chromatography is not acceptable; reprocessing should rarely be needed, must follow written procedures, and each result must be kept for review; lab records must contain complete data, e.g., notebooks, worksheets and instrument outputs such as spectra.
system_implications: By analogy: when the eBMR or a connected system recalculates or reprocesses data (yield recalculation, potency-adjusted quantities, re-evaluated in-line/PAT data), every result version is kept with inputs, parameters, user, time and justification; recalculation is permitted only in SOP-defined cases; reviewers see the full history, not just the final value.
verification_test: Recalculate a yield after correcting an input -> both results retained with reasons and visible in review; reprocess a PAT spectrum -> original and reprocessed results and parameters retained.

requirement: Suspected or known falsification or alteration of CGMP records must be fully investigated within the CGMP quality system, whatever the source or intent, to establish its impact on patients, on product quality and on the reliability of data, find the root cause and ensure corrective action; it cannot be handled informally. FDA also invites reports of suspected DI issues by email to its drug information address.
system_implications: Allow a DI concern to be raised as a deviation/investigation linked to affected batches, users and time windows; preserve evidence (affected records and audit trails locked against archival purge or disposition until closure); provide user-activity and change-history reports to scope the investigation.
verification_test: Open a DI investigation for a user and date range -> the system lists all records that user created or changed in the range; linked batches are flagged and cannot be purged until closure.

reference: Q16; binding basis 211.25
requirement: Staff should be trained, as part of routine CGMP training, to prevent and to detect data integrity problems; FDA links this to 211.25 (education, training and experience for assigned duties).
system_implications: Optional design control: grant GMP roles (entry, verification, review, release, administration) only while current training, including DI training, is recorded; reviewer training covers audit-trail review. Gating roles on training status is a firm choice, not an FDA statement.
verification_test: A user whose DI training has lapsed attempts to verify a step -> blocked or flagged per SOP; training status appears in the access report.

reference: Q17 and footnote 14; binding basis 211.180(c)
requirement: Electronic communications that support CGMP activities are CGMP records open to FDA review (an email approving batch release is FDA's example), and FDA also reviews non-CGMP records that contain CGMP information (footnote 14). Firms must permit inspection and review, and copying of records including electronic data (211.180(c)).
system_implications: Record GMP decisions and approvals (release, deviations, holds) inside the eBMR with e-signatures rather than by email or chat; comments and messages within the eBMR are retained with audit trails as part of the record; any approval received by email is attached to and retained with the batch record; inspection exports include these items.
verification_test: Batch release can only be recorded through an in-system e-signature; comments linked to a batch appear in the batch export and inspection copy.

reference: Q18 and Introduction; binding basis 211.22(a), 211.192
requirement: FDA encourages remediation that establishes the scope and root causes of DI problems, assesses their potential effects (including on submission data) with a scientifically sound risk assessment, and puts in place a management strategy with a global corrective action plan; this may involve a third-party auditor, moving responsible individuals out of positions of influence over CGMP data, stronger quality oversight, enhanced computer systems and mechanisms such as anonymous reporting and data governance. The Introduction expects risk-based DI strategies covering system design, operation and monitoring, backed by management and a quality culture that encourages reporting.
system_implications: Support scope assessment with per-user and per-period change-history reports across batches and sites; allow immediate role revocation; allow tighter controls (e.g., added verification steps) to be deployed as CAPA through configuration under change control; keep a documented DI risk assessment of eBMR workflows, reviewed periodically.
verification_test: Revoke a user's GMP rights -> effective at once across sites and logged; a scope report runs across all batches for a given user and period.

reference: Q1a (life cycle through disposition), Background (data secure until disposition), Q8 footnote 13 (deletion/amendment/exclusion risks), Q12, Q1c, Q3; binding basis 211.68(b), 211.180, 11.10(e)
requirement: Data should be protected from creation until disposition after the retention period (Q1a, Background); FDA names unauthorized or undetected deletion, amendment or exclusion as risks to data (footnote 13); required data should not be changeable without a record (Q12); audit trails cover deletions (Q1c); each workflow, including any that can remove data, is an intended use to validate (Q3).
system_implications: No workflow deletes or hides GMP data before its retention period ends; 'delete' in the UI is implemented as void/invalidate with reason, keeping the data; physical purge only after retention expiry through an authorized, documented disposition that records what was disposed and who approved it; database-level deletions prevented or detected.
verification_test: Try to delete a GMP entry through the UI and the API -> only void-with-reason is possible; attempt disposition of a batch still within retention -> blocked; disposition after expiry produces a disposition record.
